report:
Bottom line: the better answer is **no**—for tinnitus as the primary problem, ginkgo extract has not shown reliable benefit over placebo. The 2022 Cochrane review found “no evidence” that *Ginkgo biloba* improves tinnitus versus placebo, with low-certainty safety data and few serious harms reported: https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013514.pub2/full. This matches the AAO-HNSF tinnitus guideline position that clinicians should not recommend ginkgo or other dietary supplements for persistent, bothersome tinnitus: https://www.entnet.org/resource/aao-hnsf-cpg-tinnitus-press-release-fact-sheet/.

Why the confusion? An older systematic review argued standardized EGb 761 might be an evidence-based option, but it noted mixed trial results and methodological flaws; later, broader evidence synthesis did not confirm benefit: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/. Some positive studies involve specific extracts, non-primary tinnitus outcomes, or populations such as dementia, so they don’t generalize well to typical tinnitus care.

Safety is not trivial: NCCIH summarizes ginkgo’s evidence and cautions about side effects/interactions, especially bleeding risk with anticoagulants/antiplatelets and around surgery: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo. If tinnitus is new, one-sided, pulsatile, or with hearing loss/neurologic symptoms, seek medical evaluation rather than self-treating.
